title: Unto the mountains (Psalm 121)
hook: "He that keepeth Israel doth neither slumber nor sleep"

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm one thirty, a cry from the depths. Your line was out of the depths. Did you say one honest word from a low place? Today, we look up. Day three hundred twenty-five.

In some Jewish homes, a small printed card hangs near a newborn's crib. Others keep the same words folded in a wallet for a long drive, or tucked into a suitcase. The words are eight short verses, and they turn on one plain fact about people: sooner or later, guards doze and parents nod off. Nobody can keep watch forever. The psalm on the card says there is a keeper who can. It starts with a traveler looking up at the hills. Today: Psalm one twenty-one.
screen: `A CARD BY THE CRIB.` → `GUARDS DOZE, PARENTS NOD OFF.` → `A KEEPER WHO DOESN'T.`

segments.voice: It's another Song of Ascents, often read as a pilgrim's song. A traveler on the road to Jerusalem looks up at the hills ahead. "I will lift up mine eyes unto the mountains: from whence shall my help come?" Some readers hear worry in the question: hills are where danger can hide on a long road. And the answer comes straight back: my help comes from the Lord, maker of heaven and earth. Not from the mountains. From the One who made them. Then the psalm's great promise: "Behold, He that keepeth Israel doth neither slumber nor sleep." The Hebrew word is shomer: a keeper, a guard, a watchman. It's the word for a guard: someone who stays alert while others rest. In just eight verses, forms of that word appear six times. The Lord is your keeper. He'll keep you from all evil. He'll keep your going out and your coming in, from now and forever. The sun won't strike you by day, nor the moon by night. That's why many Jews say this psalm for protection: before a journey, for a woman giving birth, at a sickbed. And Hasidic teachers found a hidden reading in the opening question. From where, me-ayin, can also be heard as from ayin, from nothingness. In that reading, help begins at the moment a person admits there is nothing left. And under it stands the psalm's promise: a keeper who stays awake when we can't.
screen: `EYES LIFTED TO THE MOUNTAINS.` · `HELP FROM THE MAKER OF HEAVEN.` · `SHOMER: THE KEEPER.` · `ME-AYIN: FROM NOTHING.` · then, large: `HE DOESN'T SLEEP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a hill or the horizon. If you can see one from where you are, a hill, a skyline, the edge of the sky, look at it. If not, close your eyes and picture a range of mountains far off. Settle, and breathe. Lift your eyes, literally. Notice how different it feels to look up and out instead of down. Ask the psalm's question quietly: where will my help come from? Think of the people you're watching over. Picture them kept, even while you sleep. If you pray, you can say the psalm's promise. The bell holds the time.
Unto the mountains. Psalm one twenty-one: I lift my eyes and ask where help will come from, and the answer is a keeper who neither slumbers nor sleeps.
Your line: he doesn't sleep. Tonight, when you put down the worries you're keeping watch over, let someone else hold the night shift. Day three hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Many Jews recite Psalm 121 before travel, at a sickbed and for protection in childbirth; it is often printed on cards or plaques placed near a newborn, and it is part of the Shabbat afternoon psalms in some communities.

what it means: a promise that someone keeps watch when you can't, on every journey.

what a scholar hears: the heading is shir la-ma'alot, slightly different from the other Songs of Ascents, the root sh-m-r runs through the psalm, and Hasidic readers hear me-ayin as 'from nothingness'.
